after: ## Issues at global, national and local level
alt: Three stacked cards narrow the topic: globally, how fast to cut emissions and who pays, with the Paris Agreement aim of well below 2°C and 1.5°C; nationally, how to produce electricity from coal, gas, nuclear, hydro, solar or wind; locally, rising bills, a new mine or wind farm, or a school wasting electricity.
caption: Turn a broad topic into a specific problem at global, national and local level.

after: ## Issues at global, national and local level
alt: Paired definitions: mitigation reduces the causes of climate change while adaptation copes with its effects, such as flood defences; renewable resources such as wind and sunlight are replaced naturally while coal, oil and gas run out. Energy security is reliable, affordable energy without depending too much on others.
caption: Mitigation tackles causes; adaptation copes with effects.

alt: A spectrum from strong, fast cuts to stressing the cost of fast change. Low-lying island states sit at the fast end because rising seas threaten their land; many developing countries argue those who industrialised first should do more; oil, gas and coal earners stress lost jobs and income. The views differ because of who carries the cost and when.
caption: Perspectives on climate action often differ over who pays and when, not over the science.

alt: A balance weighs Germany’s closure of its last three nuclear power stations on 15 April 2023. Supporters pointed to safety and waste risks; critics argued nuclear is low-carbon and closure could mean burning more fossil fuel. The evaluation asks about each side’s evidence, reasoning and vested interest.
caption: People within one country can disagree about the same energy decision.

alt: A loop of five stages: hotter summers lead to more demand for air conditioning, higher electricity use, more emissions if the power comes from fossil fuels, a stronger greenhouse effect, and hotter summers again.
caption: In a feedback loop, a consequence feeds back to strengthen its own cause.

alt: A drought branches into three consequences: food prices rise for city families, farmers’ income is cut, and hydro-power dams produce less.
caption: The same cause falls differently on different groups.

alt: Two sources compared. A fictional energy company leaflet calls its gas plant clean and green but has a vested interest, uses emotive language and gives no emissions figures. IPCC reports summarise many reviewed studies but give projections as ranges. Below, a five-point reliability checklist.
caption: Even a reliable source has limits; a weak one needs independent support.

alt: Three columns of actions: globally the Paris Agreement and the COP27 loss and damage fund; nationally carbon taxes, renewable subsidies and building codes; locally community solar, insulation and school energy audits. Below, a general rooftop solar subsidy cuts emissions but mainly helps wealthier districts, while a targeted subsidy is fairer but costs more per panel.
caption: Choosing an action means deciding which criterion matters most.
